caption: Control Group
description: The Control Group object describes an operating system mechanism that groups processes so that resource limits, accounting, and isolation can be applied to them as a unit. For example, a Linux control group (cgroup) or a Windows job object. Container runtimes build on control groups, but they also group processes outside containers, such as system services and user sessions. A Windows job object is unrelated to the job object, which describes a scheduled job or task.
name: control_group

name.description: The name of the control group. For example, the last component of a Linux cgroup path such as sshd.service, or the name of a named Windows job object.

path.description: The hierarchical path of the control group, on platforms that organize control groups in a hierarchy. For a Linux cgroup, this is the path relative to the root of the cgroup hierarchy, as reported in /proc/[pid]/cgroup when read from the initial cgroup namespace, without the mount point of the cgroup filesystem. For example: /system.slice/sshd.service. A process inside a cgroup namespace, such as a container, sees a path relative to its namespace root instead, often just /.

uid.description: The unique identifier of the control group, as assigned by the operating system. For a Linux cgroup v2, this is the 64-bit cgroup ID, which is the inode number of the cgroup directory and is the value returned by the bpf_get_current_cgroup_id eBPF helper.

uid_numeric.description:
The uid attribute in numeric form, where the operating system assigns a numeric identifier. For example, the 64-bit Linux cgroup ID.
Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.

references.description: Linux kernel documentation: Control Group v2
